# Prescriptive lessons — jerry-bergonzi × melodic-rhythms-vol-4

## sus4

Bergonzi reserves the dominant sus4 chord as a pedagogical harmonic backdrop rather than a performance target: its absence of avoid notes makes it the ideal canvas for hearing pure key-center sound. Both sus4 lessons serve systematic practice contexts — modal transposition and scale-sequence familiarization — rather than prescribing sus4 as an improvisational choice over changes.

- [ch.28 p.113] Play modal scale sequences over a dominant sus4 chord to remove avoid-note constraints and hear the pure sound of the key without harmonic interference.
- [ch.28 p.113] When rhythmizing scale sequences, start the pattern from every degree of the scale (modal transposition) over a sus4 chord — making it the recommended harmonic backdrop for systematic modal transposition practice.

## dom7

Bergonzi's dominant-context teaching is the spine of the entire book: nearly every rhythmic principle — displacement, gear-switching, polyrhythm, grammar constraints — is exemplified over dom7. The lessons cluster into five coherent areas: (1) eighth-note pocket and subdivision hierarchy; (2) displacement and superimposition as melodic devices; (3) time-zone/gear taxonomy and switching; (4) polyrhythm construction methods; and (5) rhythmic grammar rules governing phrase shape and density. The unifying thread is that rhythmic vocabulary is context-neutral — these techniques apply over any chord, but dom7 is the demonstration ground throughout.

**Pocket and subdivision**

- [ch.18 p.77] Eighth notes over a dominant groove must coexist with the triplet feel — sometimes by laying back or applying a lob — rather than collapsing into or fighting the triplet pulse.
- [ch.18 p.77] *(proscriptive)* Do not play eighth notes as literal triplets; the triplet feel is internalized and felt, not mechanically applied to articulation.
- [ch.18 p.77] Practice explicit triplet rhythms on a tune, then switch to eighth notes on the same tune, to internalize the pocket through felt contrast.
- [ch.19 p.83] Set the metronome between 50 and 60 on the half note and repeat a line until triplets feel natural with eighth-note articulation.

**Displacement and superimposition**

- [ch.1 p.9-10] Treat consecutive note groupings as independent of bar lines — play a fixed number of notes within, over, or through the bar; internal mental grouping affects articulation even when invisible to the listener.
- [ch.1 p.10] A five-note grouping may be played over 1 beat, 1½ beats, 2 beats, 3 beats, or 4 beats — the same melodic cell flexibly rescaled to any duration.
- [ch.2 p.16] Displace one-bar rhythms by ½ beat, 1½ beats, or 2½ beats to produce perceptually distinct rhythmic patterns.
- [ch.3 p.26] For four-note groupings, displacement positions #6, #7, and #8 (starting on the "and" of 3, beat 4, or the "and" of 4) automatically anticipate the next chord — by approaching its notes, stating it directly, or letting the final eighth note sound it. Positions #5–#7 apply the same rule to five-note groups.
- [ch.3 p.27 / ch.15 p.69, 71] Superimpose odd-meter groupings (3/4, 5/4, 7/4, 9/4, 11/4) over a 4/4 foundation as a systematic method for generating rhythmic variety; the 5/4-over-4/4 cycle aligns on bar 6, the 7/4 cycle on bar 8.
- [ch.9 p.47] When practicing two consecutive eighth-note triplet groups, sound only four of the six available subdivisions to develop rhythmic precision and selective articulation.
- [ch.10 p.49] Internalize triplet groupings by playing a fixed four-note melody starting on different beats within triplet groupings before attempting free triplet improvisation.
- [ch.10 p.50] After structured triplet-grouping drills, escalate to randomized practice as the final stage of mastery.
- [ch.13 p.62] Convert consecutive eighth-note exercises into sixteenth-note (double-time) exercises by doubling up; repeat the resulting 2/4 phrase twice to fill a 4/4 bar.
- [ch.13 p.63] Play 3/4 rhythmic phrases over 4/4 tunes (hemiola) to ensure phrases begin from various beats rather than always landing on beat one; four bars of 3/4 equals three bars of 4/4.
- [ch.13 p.63] Practice hemiola with a play-along while the right foot taps beat one and the left foot taps beat 3, combined with singing, to physically internalize the cross-rhythm.
- [ch.15 p.68-69] Internalize 3/4-over-4/4 by first practicing 3/4 rhythms exclusively, then combining two for a 6/4 cell, then combining four for longer lines, and finally playing random 3/4-over-4/4 without any programmed sequence.
- [ch.16 p.72] Generate a 5/4 mirror rhythm (hemioval) by restating the same rhythm on beat 2-and that was started on beat 1; generate a 7/4 mirror rhythm by restating on beat 3-and.
- [ch.17 p.74] Take any of the 22 one-bar 4/4 rhythms from Chapter 2 and play them over a 3/4 tune; then combine two of those rhythms into longer polyrhythmic phrases over 3/4.

**Time-zone / gear system**

- [ch.19 p.82] Expand vocabulary by adapting any line to five distinct time zones or gears: quarter-note triplet, eighth-note, triplet, sixteenth-note, and sextuplet.
- [ch.19 p.83] When recasting an eighth-note line into triplet gear, leave off either the first four or the last four notes of an eight-note phrase to make the line fit comfortably in triplet subdivision.
- [ch.20 p.86] Switch between time zones randomly and spontaneously during improvisation rather than programming gear changes, in order to develop transferable fluency.
- [ch.21 p.88] Master one time zone at a time by playing through an entire play-along track in that zone exclusively, then master the next, then freely vary between zones.
- [ch.24 p.106] Take any fixed group of notes and reinterpret it across different beat spans — from one beat through four beats, or compressed into 1½ beats — as a perceptual strategy for dissolving the strangeness of odd tuplets.
- [ch.27 p.111] At fast tempos, collapse the felt pulse to "two" or "one" beat per measure to escape the eighth-note trap — even perceiving a fast tune as a ballad.
- [ch.27 p.111] Use varied metronome placements to develop time independence: on 2 and 4, on 1 and 3, on just 3, on just 4, or on the "and" of 2 and 4.
- [ch.27 p.112] Practice without a metronome by meditating on a tempo, hearing quarter notes internally, then adding triplets or other rhythms mentally; relaxation is the cognitive prerequisite.

**Polyrhythm construction**

- [ch.22 p.91] Internalize 5-against-4 polyrhythm through repetition and articulation variation before moving to construction methods.
- [ch.22 p.92] Build 9-against-4 by adding one note to each bar of eighth notes, or simply adding two notes at the end of the original eight-note line.
- [ch.22 p.92] Build 10-against-4 by subtracting six notes from an eight-note line; build 12-against-4 by subtracting four notes.
- [ch.23 p.94-95] Play scale sequences in odd groupings of 5, 7, or 9 over any harmonic context; nine-note sequences are played over four beats or two beats depending on tempo.
- [ch.23 p.100] Treat polyrhythmic mastery as a long-range pursuit, not a weekly drill.
- [ch.23 p.102-103] Deploy septuplets and nonuplets over two, three, or four beats, selecting the metric span by context.
- [ch.24 p.105] Start polyrhythmic exercises one beat early or one beat late so that the pattern crosses the 4/4 bar line, building polyrhythmic independence.
- [ch.28 p.113] Generate groups of seven by leaving out one note from two groups of four within a scale sequence.
- [ch.28 p.114] Add rests within scale sequences as an active rhythmizing move.
- [ch.28 p.114] Vary scale sequences by ascending or descending within them, and by skipping to any note in the scale to start the sequence.
- [ch.28 p.115] Familiarize yourself with a sequence first, then work through the possibilities with creative freedom, composing 12 modal sequences and playing them over backing tracks.
- [ch.21 p.88 / ch.28 p.115] Compose your own scale and intervallic sequences in a time zone as the benchmark of genuine mastery — not merely executing given exercises.

**Rhythmic grammar and phrase shaping**

- [ch.1 p.7] Develop awareness of which rhythms you are using and where you are in the bar; more notes per bar is not better than fewer — only different.
- [ch.25 p.107] First isolate downbeat playing, then upbeat playing, then mix the two on a single tune to develop fluid quarter-note soloing.
- [ch.27 p.110] Play solos using only half notes, quarter notes, and dotted quarters to create breathing room and enable rhythmic dialogue with the rhythm section.
- [ch.27 p.110] Play just accents through a tune (as if part of a horn section), then slowly fill in around those accents across several choruses.
- [ch.29 p.116] *(proscriptive)* Never start on beat one. Never end on beat one.
- [ch.29 p.116] Anticipate chord arrivals at offsets of ½ beat, 1 beat, 1½ beats, 2 beats, 2½ beats, and 3 beats as explicit rhythmic grammar practice.
- [ch.29 p.116] Deliberately delay resolution by 1 to 4 beats as a rhythmic grammar tool over any chord change.
- [ch.29 p.116 / ch.27 p.110] Alternate between passages predominantly in eighth notes and passages containing no eighth notes at all — avoiding relentless eighth-note density.
- [ch.29 p.116] Treat silence and phrase endings as active compositional events: leave periods at the ends of sentences and paragraphs, know when to end a solo, and listen to the rests.
